questions.question: Distinguish between a movement along the supply curve and a shift of the supply curve, and give the single test question that separates them.
questions.expected_answer: A movement along the curve happens when the good's own price changes — sellers respond to the new price on the same curve, a change in quantity supplied. A shift happens when a non-price factor (input costs, technology, taxes, number of producers, natural events like disease or weather) changes what sellers offer at every price. The test: did the good's own price cause the change? If yes, move along the curve; if no, shift the whole curve.

questions.question: Explain why neither a price above equilibrium nor a price below equilibrium can persist in a free market.
questions.expected_answer: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — a surplus. Unsold stock pressures sellers to cut prices, so the price falls toward equilibrium. Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied — a shortage. Competing buyers bid the price up. Only at equilibrium is there no surplus or shortage and therefore no pressure on the price to change.

questions.question: Work through the bird flu case in your own words: which curve shifts, why, in which direction, and what happens to equilibrium price and quantity.
questions.expected_answer: The outbreak strikes the farms, so it is a supply-side change, and it was caused by disease rather than the egg price — therefore the whole supply curve shifts. It shifts left because fewer eggs can be offered at every price. Demand stays put since incomes and tastes are unchanged. At the old price a shortage appears, buyers bid the price up, and the new equilibrium has a higher price with a smaller quantity of eggs traded.
